title: Macros
summary: Chapter 11 introduces Vim macros: recording keystrokes into a register with q{register} and replaying them with @{register} or @@. It contrasts executing a macro in series, where one failure aborts the remaining queued repetitions, with executing it in parallel via :normal @a or :argdo normal @a, where each invocation is independent. It also teaches repeatable macro design (normalize the cursor, prefer robust motions, let failed motions abort safely), playback with a count, appending with qA, editing a macro as plain text, and using the expression register with a counter to number list items.

commands.meaning: Begin recording keystrokes into the named register
commands.evidence: The q key functions both as the “record” button and the “stop” button. To begin recording our keystrokes, we type q{register}, giving the address of the register where we want to save the macro. We can tell that we’ve done it right if the word “recording” appears in the status line. Every command that we execute will be captured, right up until we press q again to stop recording.

Pressing qa begins recording and saves our macro into register a. We then perform two changes on the first line: appending a semicolon and prepending the word var. Having completed both of those changes, we press q to stop recording our macro (qⓘ).

commands.meaning: Execute the macro stored in the named register
commands.evidence: The @{register} command executes the contents of the specified register (see @ⓘ). We can also use @@, which repeats the macro that was invoked most recently.

commands.meaning: Repeat the macro most recently invoked
commands.evidence: The @{register} command executes the contents of the specified register (see @ⓘ). We can also use @@, which repeats the macro that was invoked most recently.

commands.meaning: Play the macro in register a with a count, repeating it ten times
commands.evidence: Suppose that the macro was stored in the a register. Rather than executing @a ten times, we could prefix it with a count: 10@a. The beauty of this technique is that we can be unscrupulous about how many times we execute this macro. Don’t care for counting? It doesn’t matter! We could execute 100@a or even 1000@a, and it would produce the same result.

commands.meaning: Record a one-off macro in register q that runs ; then .
commands.evidence: We can simulate this by recording one of the simplest possible macros: qq;.q. Here, qq tells Vim to record the following keystrokes and save them to the q register. Then we type our commands ;. and finish recording the macro by pressing q one final time. Now we can execute the macro with a count: 11@q. This executes ;. eleven times.

commands.meaning: Append keystrokes to the existing macro in register a instead of overwriting it
commands.evidence: If we type qa, then Vim will record our keystrokes, saving them into register a by overwriting the existing contents of that register. If we type qA, then Vim will append our keystrokes to the existing contents of register a.

commands.meaning: Inspect the contents of register a
Run the macro once on each line of the selected range
commands.evidence: The :normal @a command tells Vim to execute the macro once for each line in the selection. Just as before, the macro succeeds on the first two lines and then aborts on line three, but it doesn’t stall there this time—it completes the job. Why?

commands.meaning: Run the macro once in every buffer in the argument list
Advance to the next file in the argument list; failure on the last file aborts a series macro
commands.evidence: While we could run 3@a to execute the macro on each of the remaining files in the buffer list, there’s no need to be so precise about it. When we reach the last buffer in the argument list, the :next command fails and the macro aborts. So, rather than specifying an exact count, we only have to ensure that we provide a number that’s large enough: 22 will do, and it’s easy to type.

commands.meaning: Paste the contents of register a below the current line as plain text
Yank from the cursor to the end of the line into register a, character-wise
commands.evidence: When we run the command 0 followed by "ay$, we yank every character on that line except for the carriage return. Having captured everything that we want to keep into register a, we can then run dd to delete the line. This will end up in the default register, but we won’t use it.

commands.meaning: Insert the value of variable i via the expression register in Insert mode
commands.evidence: The :echo command is fine for revealing the value that is assigned to a variable, but ideally we want to insert that value into the document. We can do that using the expression register. In Tip 16, we saw that the expression register can be used to do simple sums and to insert the result into the document. We can insert the value stored in variable i just by running <C-r>=i<CR> in Insert mode.

concepts.name: Play back with a count
concepts.evidence: The Dot Formula can be an efficient editing strategy for a small number of repeats, but it can’t be executed with a count. Overcome this limitation by recording a cheap one-off macro and playing it back with a count.

concepts.name: Append commands to a macro
concepts.evidence: Sometimes we miss a vital step when we record a macro. There’s no need to re-record the whole thing from scratch. Instead, we can tack extra commands onto the end of an existing macro.

problems.evidence: Being able to paste a macro into the document, edit it right there, and then yank it back into a register and execute it is very handy. But the register can be fussy to work with for the reasons noted in Keyboard Codes in Macros. If you only have to append a command at the end of your macro, following the procedure outlined in Tip 69, is simpler.
